Subsequent FECA htigation in the D.C. Circuit makes clear that Akins 
remains the controlling authority, at least in FECA actions. Applying Akins, 
that court found in Campaign Legal Center v. FEC, 31 F.4th 781 (D.C. Cir. 
2022) that plaintiffs, a voter and a watchdog group, had suffered informational 
injury under FECA because Correct the Record (a 2016 Hillary Clinton super 
PAC) and Hillary for America had failed to disclose information about 
coordinated in-kind contributions.
In Campaign Legal Center & Democracy 21 v. FEC, 952 F.3d 352 (D.C. 
Cir. 2020), the court again found an injury, finding that “The law is settled that 
a denial of access to information qualifies as an injury in fact where a statute 
(on the claimants’ reading) requires that information be pubficly disclosed and 
there is no reason to doubt their claim that the information would help them.” 
(quoting Envtl. Def. Fund v. EPA, 922 F.3d 446, 452 (D.C. Cir. 2019)
2. 
Novel Injuries. Subsequent cases have, however, caste doubt on how 
creative Congress can be when creating interests whose invasion will count as 
injuries for purposes of Article III. In TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 141 S.Ct. 
2190 (2021) the Court found that some plaintiffs lacked Article III standing 
under a statutory cause of action included in the Fair Credit Reporting Act 
because they had not suffered concrete and particularized injuries. The Court 
held that in assessing the concreteness of statutory injuries, courts should look 
to whether “whether the alleged injury to the plaintiff has a ‘close relationship’ 
to a harm ‘traditionally’ recognized as providing a basis for a lawsuit in 
American courts.” Id. at 2204. While tangible harms (physical/economic injury) 
qualify, intangibles like “reputational harms, disclosure of private information, 
and intrusion upon seclusion” “can also be concrete” but must often must “a 
close relationship to harms traditionally recognized as providing a basis for 
lawsuits.” Id.
Congress’s views as to the concreteness of a harm can be “instructive,’ but 
while “Congress may ‘elevate’ harms that ‘exist’ in the real world before 
Congress recognized them to actionable legal status, it may not simply enact 
an injury into existence, using its lawmaking power to transform something 
that is not remotely harmful into something that is.” (quoting Hagy v. Demers 
& Adams, 882 F.3d 616, 622 (CA6 2018)).
